THE PLAYER’S HANDBOOK · CUSTOM RULES

Eleven a side.
A new kind of tactics.

This is our custom Football Chess variation: a 14 × 17 pitch, four-square goals in files f–i, six-by-three keeper boxes in files e–j, and eleven footballers per side. Each team has one king, one queen, two rooks, two bishops, two knights, and three pawns.

The starting shape

Both teams use the same formation rotated 180°. Ivory starts with the king on g2, pawns on f4/h4/j4, wide rooks on b4/m4, bishops on c5/l5, knights on d8/j7, and the queen on g5. The kickoff queen moves to the centre: g9 for Ivory or h9 for Obsidian. You can rearrange your own half before kickoff.

The pawns form a screen immediately in front of the three-rank box; the king patrols behind them and the bishops support the flanks. The wide rooks initially link to the nearest screen pawn. An eleven-square crossfield switch opens after that passing lane is cleared, with the usual long-pass accuracy penalty. Opposite-colour bishops connect the wings; moving the supporting knight from j7 opens the right bishop’s forward diagonal. The advanced knight on d8 can receive directly from the queen’s normal g5 position.

01 · Shape the play

The attacker can dribble once and move another player without the ball once, plus use one shared pawn-or-king bonus, in any order. The defender then has one regular move or tackle plus a shared pawn-or-king bonus, before the attacker kicks. End positioning to skip unused actions.

02 · Move like chess

Use chess movement patterns with ten movement points without the ball, or eight when dribbling. Entering a box square costs two points; another square costs one. A move entirely inside a box reaches at most five squares off the ball or four when dribbling. Kings and pawns still move one square; knights make one L-shaped jump over other pieces, including while dribbling. Pawns can move forward, backward, left, or right.

03 · Keep the ball moving

Kicks follow the carrier’s kicking directions. A short pass stops at the first piece in its path; an empty target leaves a loose ball. A friendly back-pass to the king requires an immediate kick: the king cannot hold or dribble it.

04 · Pick your finish

Aim at any legal goal target in files f–i. The shooter commits the target, then the defending king may move one legal square or hold before the shot resolves. Outfield players may dribble into either box, move there without the ball, or receive a teammate’s pass there. Pass-and-run cannot enter a box. The four squares directly in front of each goal are reserved for its goalkeeper. A king cannot enter the opponent’s box.

Move, dribble, or send the ball

ActionWhat moves?When?
Move without ballThe selected player moves. The ball stays unless the move collects it or wins a tackle.One off-ball move in attack; one regular move or tackle in defence
DribbleThe carrier and ball move together, using that piece’s movement pattern.One independent action in ordinary attacking positioning; it does not spend the off-ball move
Pawn or King bonusOne pawn without the ball moves one cardinal square, or the king without the ball moves one adjacent square. It may collect a loose ball; no dribble or tackle.One shared bonus per attacking or defending positioning turn, separate from the regular action and keeper shot reaction
Pass / shootThe carrier stays in place and kicks the ball. A teammate receives a pass; an empty square leaves it loose; a goal cell declares a shot.Kicking phase, kickoff, or mandatory keeper release; a goal kick must be a pass

Attacking dribble, off-ball move, and pawn-or-king bonus are separate and optional, in any order. Dribble then move a teammate, or move a teammate then dribble. Each allowance is used once. The shared bonus repositions either a pawn or the king without the ball: one cardinal square for a pawn, one adjacent square in any direction for a king. Either may collect a loose ball, but the bonus cannot dribble or tackle. Using it on a pawn spends the king’s bonus too, and using it on the king spends the pawn’s bonus. The keeper’s later shot reaction remains separate. Every carrier, including a pawn, gets only one dribble per attacking positioning turn. Collecting your own previous pass also spends that dribble, so you cannot pass, chase, and carry again before the defender responds. Collecting another player’s loose pass can still leave your single dribble available. The defender then positions before the attacker kicks. A turnover resets all allowances for the new attacker.

Keep the attack moving

The stalling rule applies only in the possessing team’s own half. There, advance the ball at least four net squares toward the opponent’s goal within three completed possession rounds, shoot at the opponent’s goal, or finish a round at midfield or beyond. A round is attacking positioning, defending positioning, then the kick; the king’s forced back-pass release completes the same round. Individual player moves do not each count as a round. Progress is measured along the pitch at the end of the round, so sideways passing and moving forward then back cannot reset the count.

Four squares of net forward progress reset the checkpoint and grant three fresh rounds. The progress panel shows what remains and warns before the last round. After three rounds without enough progress or a shot, the opponent’s nearest eligible player takes an indirect free kick at the nearest free legal square to the ball. Nobody is displaced. Both teams resettle with the taker locked, then the taker passes; a direct goal is unavailable.

Midfield and the opponent’s half have no forward-progress deadline. A completed round ending there clears the own-half count; returning to your own half starts a fresh three-round window. Crossing midfield and passing back within the same round does not clear an existing count. A change of possession or a restart also clears it. Kickoff, protected restart positioning, and the restart kick do not spend the allowance. A pass into space still counts as a round; a complete positioning round with the ball left loose also counts. A shot at the opponent’s goal resets the window.

Two additional pace rules apply throughout the pitch. One player may dribble in four completed ordinary possession rounds; attempting a fifth carry awards the nearest eligible opponent an indirect free kick near the ball. A pass into space and collection by the same player count as carrying, so self-passes cannot bypass the limit. Skipping a carry does not reset it. A different teammate must take control, or the team must shoot, lose possession, or reach a restart to reset the count. The warning panel shows completed carrying rounds and warns before the limit.

Returning to the same ball square and controlling player for a third time in a repeated short route without new forward progress also awards that indirect free kick against the possessing side. The game checks completed-round checkpoints for cycles lasting one, two, or three rounds. A new furthest forward completed-round point breaks the cycle. Off-ball shuffles and the opponent’s defensive replies do not count as an offence. Both teams then resettle with the nearest eligible taker locked, following the same protected sequence as other indirect free kicks. These carrying and repetition limits are custom game rules.

Each piece has movement and kicking patterns

PieceOff-ball moveDribblePass / shoot
KingOne square in any directionOne square in any directionStraight or diagonal rays, like a queen
QueenStraight or diagonal, up to 10 movement pointsStraight or diagonal, up to 8 movement pointsStraight or diagonal rays
RookHorizontal or vertical, up to 10 movement pointsHorizontal or vertical, up to 8 movement pointsHorizontal or vertical rays; stronger long-shot accuracy
BishopDiagonal, up to 10 movement pointsDiagonal, up to 8 movement pointsDiagonal rays
KnightOne L-shaped jumpOne L-shaped jumpOne L-shaped kick
PawnOne square forward, back, left, or rightOne square forward, back, left, or rightForward, backward, left, or right rays

All outfield players can enter, cross or leave either team’s box during an ordinary dribble or off-ball move, and receive a teammate’s pass there. Pass-and-run cannot enter a box. Passing into space and then collecting your own pass also cannot be used to enter a box from outside. The four goal-mouth squares directly in front of each goal (f1–i1 and f17–i17) belong only to that goal’s defending king; every other player is barred. The king cannot enter the opponent’s box. Queen, rook and bishop moves have a ten-point budget without the ball and eight points when dribbling. Every entered box square costs two points and every other entered square one; the starting square is free. A dribble entirely inside a box can enter at most four squares. Mixed routes add both costs: three outside squares plus two box squares cost seven points. Shorter piece patterns still apply. Ray kicks have no ten-square cap; knight kicks make one L-shaped jump. Long passes lose accuracy. Ordinary passes stop at the first player. A non-jumping shot cannot cross a teammate; an opponent in its path may block it. A king inside its own box uses saving mechanics instead of body blocking.

Choose Pass & run before a kick to request an optional run by the passer after an accurate pass reaches a teammate other than the king. The run uses the following attacking turn’s normal off-ball allowance, cannot tackle or collect the ball, and cannot enter a box. The receiver’s separate dribble and the shared pawn-or-king bonus remain available. Skip run keeps the normal off-ball allowance. Inaccurate or intercepted passes grant no run. A pass to the king always requires immediate release instead.

Each straight or diagonal movement step is one square before applying the box cost. Tackle reach and pass range still count the larger horizontal or vertical displacement: an eight-by-eight diagonal is eight squares. Shot accuracy and goalkeeper coverage use straight-line distance to the goal plane, half a square beyond the end row.

Knights can jump into both teams’ goal boxes during ordinary dribbling or off-ball movement, and can receive passes there. A knight scores when one L-shaped kick lands in a goal cell; for example, e16 to the upper F goal, or g16 to the upper F goal from inside the box. Its scoring chance uses the standard distance, angle and keeper model, with no scoring multiplier. A keeper inside its own box still reacts first. A midfield knight cannot shoot directly at goal. Unreachable goal targets show “—”.

A finish depends on the whole shot

Queens and knights may choose a disguised shot when their normal kicking pattern reaches two legal squares in the opponent’s goal. Both targets are shown to the keeper, but the actual aim is chosen with equal 50/50 odds only after the keeper moves or holds. The preview averages both possible shots; each still uses its own distance, angle and blocking chances. You can turn disguise off to choose one target normally. Disguise does not extend kicking range or apply to penalties.

Closer shots give the keeper less time to react. A tight angle beside a post now carries a stronger accuracy penalty. A larger opening between the posts improves finishing: above 45° the accuracy bonus increases smoothly, reaching +25% at 90°. Shooting from central files g or h adds another 15% to raw accuracy; aiming at those files alone gives no bonus. All pieces also receive a 15% raw accuracy increase. These accuracy rewards apply before the 98% on-target cap. The keeper’s position matters along the actual shot path: a shot travelling farther from the keeper is harder to save. Knights use the same scoring model without a multiplier.

The model combines the chance of hitting the target with the chance of beating the keeper. The keeper’s potential save chance for an unblocked shot on target has a 90% ceiling, reduced from 94% to make good chances slightly easier to finish. Flight time, position and reach determine the actual save chance for each shot. A longer flight lets the keeper cover more ground. Kings have saving reach and an extra shot reaction only while inside their own six-by-three box. A king may step out onto the ordinary field during positioning, but cannot enter the opponent’s box. Outside its own box it is an ordinary king: no saving reach, catches, parries, or extra reaction. Its occupied square can still intercept a kick like any other piece. Re-entering its own box during ordinary positioning restores goalkeeper abilities. The blue reach area and dashed coverage line show this geometry during a shot preview.

Shots beyond three squares lose accuracy increasingly quickly. Rooks have a gentler distance penalty, giving them stronger long shots along their horizontal and vertical kicking lines. Close shots use the normal distance curve; every piece still faces angle penalties and the keeper’s reaction. Very long shots can fall to a 1% on-target chance. Passing uses its separate accuracy rule below.

You may shoot through an opponent’s occupied square. Each defender crossed by the physical shot line has a 45% chance of blocking it; two defenders give a 69.75% block chance. A block sends the ball out for a corner 85% of the time and gives the first defender possession 15% of the time. These outcomes reduce the chances of a goal, keeper save, or wide shot. A line touching only a square’s corner does not cross it. Teammates still obstruct ordinary shots. Knight kicks lob over intervening pieces and use their normal L-shaped range. A king outside its own box counts as an ordinary blocker.

After the defending king reacts or holds, an unblocked shot can score, be caught, be parried out, spill back into play, or go wide. If the keeper stops it, estimated arrival pace and the stretch needed determine whether they hold or parry it. For an opponent’s shot, 20% of parries stay in play and the rest go out for a corner. A live rebound lands uniformly on an empty square inside the defending box or within two squares of it, clipped to the pitch and excluding the four goalkeeper-only goal-mouth squares. Neither side automatically receives the ball: legal positioning and collection continue. Shot-time offside flags still apply; the shooter and teammates who were onside may chase the rebound. Shorter travel means a faster arrival and a greater chance of a parry; reaching away from the body also makes the ball harder to control. Slower, central stops are easier to hold. All shots share the same launch power; travel distance estimates arrival pace.

“Keeper parry if stopped” is conditional on a keeper save. The preview shows Loose rebound separately. Its Corner chance combines keeper parries that go out and defender deflections, without counting either twice. Live rebounds do not change the shot’s goal, caught-save or wide probabilities. Penalties retain their fixed resolution, and a keeper catching a teammate’s backward kick must still release it immediately. A parry or block out uses the aimed goal square to choose the corner side: f or g gives the left corner; h or i gives the right corner, as seen on the unrotated pitch. A disguised shot uses its actual resolved target. An own-goal attempt deflected out by the shooting team instead gives the opponents a goal kick. A long wide shot can cross a touchline or end line according to its sampled landing. A short wide shot gives a goal kick, or a corner if it was aimed toward the shooter’s own goal. Goal kicks, corners, and throw-ins all give both teams a protected positioning turn before the restart.

Offside at the moment of play

A teammate is in an offside position when they are in the opponents’ half and strictly nearer the goal line than both the ball and the second-last opponent when the ball is played. All opposing pieces count, including the king; the king is not assumed to be the last defender. Level with the ball or second-last opponent is onside, as is the halfway row. While a piece controls the ball, the dashed line previews the current limit and “!” marks a player beyond it. After a kick, loose-ball warnings use the kick-time snapshot. The kicker may chase and collect its own kick across the line; an onside teammate may also run beyond the line after the kick. Self-collection still uses the normal movement and dribble allowances.

Any attacking outfield player in the opponent’s box automatically counts as involved at a teammate’s kick. If it is offside then, the opponents immediately receive an indirect free kick, even if the ball is aimed elsewhere. Move the attacker onside or outside the box before kicking. Players defending their own box are unaffected. Other players flagged at the kick are penalised when receiving, collecting, or challenging for that ball, even if they moved back onside meanwhile. A goalkeeper save or reflex defensive shot block does not clear the snapshot, even if the defender takes possession; a subsequent deliberate controlled move or kick does. “OFF” warns of an involvement that awards an indirect free kick. This automatic box involvement is a custom grid-game rule; visual obstruction is not simulated. There is no offside directly from a goal kick, corner, or throw-in, including automatic box involvement. An offside free kick is indirect and cannot score directly.

Boundaries and restarts

An inaccurate ordinary pass longer than ten squares samples a landing around its target without clamping it to the pitch. Scatter grows with distance. Long wide shots similarly sample an extended landing. The first boundary crossed determines the restart: a touchline gives the other team a throw-in; an end line gives a goal kick when the attacker touched last, or a corner when the defender touched last. The match journal names the award.

A goal kick belongs to the defending king, placed at a free square in its own goal box. Both teams resettle first, then the king must pass into the pitch. The king stays at the restart spot during positioning and cannot dribble or shoot directly from the goal kick. Direct receipt remains exempt from offside.

Goal-kick, corner and free-kick passes may loft over one intervening player of either team. “LOFT” marks targets beyond that player. You may still pass directly to the first player; a second occupied square can receive or intercept the lofted ball, but cannot be bypassed. The taker keeps its normal kicking pattern. Throws and open-play passes retain their normal blockers; shots retain their existing blocking and direct-goal restrictions. Lofting does not improve accuracy beyond ten squares or remove offside.

Goal kicks, corners, throws, offside free kicks, and stalling free kicks all follow the same protected sequence: the team taking the restart positions first, then its opponent positions, then the restart is played. Each team may move one off-ball player and use one shared pawn-or-king bonus, or end its positioning early. The taker stays locked in place; there is no extra dribble, and tackling is unavailable until the ball is played. For a corner, first choose any teammate beyond midfield in the attacking half; the halfway row does not qualify. The selected piece moves to the nearest free legal corner square, then both teams resettle with their normal allowances. If no teammate is in the attacking half, the nearest teammate takes it automatically. Running out of selection time also chooses a legal taker automatically. Throws and free kicks keep nearest-eligible selection. Nobody is displaced.

Throw-ins

Any piece throws along straight or diagonal lines, independently of its normal kicking pattern. A throw stops at the first player, cannot score directly, and cannot target beyond ten squares. Accuracy is 100% through five squares, then 85%, 70%, 55%, 40%, and 25% at six through ten squares. An inaccurate throw may also land outside and award a new restart. The green guide marks the safe five-square range; the blue guide marks the ten-square limit.

Passing accuracy

Passes up to ten squares have 100% accuracy. Beyond ten squares, accuracy falls by ten percentage points per additional square, to a minimum of 25%. Target previews show the current odds before you kick.

Tackles, pawns, and knights

Queen, rook, and bishop tackles can reach the opposing ball carrier up to five squares away along their usual straight or diagonal capture directions. Their off-ball movement has ten points and dribbling eight, with double cost for entered box squares. Tackle reach keeps its separate five-square rule. Kings challenge one adjacent square, knights one L-shaped jump, and pawns one square on any of the four diagonals, forward or backward. After reaching the carrier, choose an allowed landing beside it; the overall start-to-landing limit remains ten squares.

A piece that can reach the opposing carrier using its tackle pattern may tackle: choose a highlighted landing square beside the carrier. With Fouls mode off, both footballers stay on the pitch: tackles against a knight succeed 50% of the time and other legal tackles 100%. The defender moves to the chosen adjacent square either way. A failed tackle leaves the knight with the ball and consumes the defender’s regular move. Pawns can tackle diagonally forward or backward using their regular action; their movement and dribbling remain one cardinal square. The pawn-or-king bonus cannot tackle or dribble. Knights can still jump over defenders while dribbling.

Fouls mode, cards and penalties

Choose Fouls mode before kickoff. It is on by default for a fresh match; an older saved match without this setting keeps it off. Every tackle in Fouls mode has a 10% foul chance: 3% without a card, 5% yellow and 2% direct red. Those card odds are percentages of all tackles and are included in the 10%. The remaining 90% are clean challenges: ordinary clean tackles win the ball, while a knight evades half of clean attempts. That makes a knight challenge 45% win, 45% evade and 10% foul overall.

Two yellows send a player off. A red removes that player for the rest of the match; goals do not restore them or clear cards. If the king is dismissed, the nearest available pawn becomes the replacement keeper, or another teammate if no pawn remains. It keeps its player ID and takes the king’s capabilities. A team with fewer than seven active players forfeits; the report keeps the goals actually scored and identifies the forfeit.

A foul is judged at the ball carrier’s square when challenged. Outside the defender’s own box, the attacking side receives a direct free kick. The nearest eligible teammate takes it, both teams resettle with the taker locked, and the restart may pass, shoot or loft a pass over one player. A foul inside the defender’s own box awards a penalty instead.

A penalty also allows the usual protected resettling turns. The taker then chooses any of the four goal targets, regardless of its normal kicking pattern. Its chance of scoring is exactly 80%, independent of distance, angle, blockers, ordinary accuracy bonuses or piece type. The keeper has no extra reaction move. The remaining 20% is a catch when the keeper is in its own box, otherwise a miss and goal kick. A foul award near full time preserves its restart and final attacking chance.

Computer difficulty

Casual reacts to the current position: it creates passing lanes, collects loose balls, protects possession and covers likely receivers. Tactical searches both teams’ replies, plans off-ball runs and receiving finishes, and weighs shots against retaining possession. It checks free pawn-or-king repositioning followed by a tackle, and favours wide attacks with a legal, onside central crossing target. It also accounts for foul and card risks. Both levels use identical piece abilities, progress rules and scoring odds. Opponent pace controls the pause between actions independently of difficulty. You can change either setting during a match.

Tactical uses handcrafted evaluation and bounded look-ahead search. It judges legal passing lanes, space to carry into, receiving chances and defensive replies from the visible board. No learned model or training is used during play.

Choose “Watch · computer vs computer” to watch both teams play automatically. Pick Casual or Tactical separately for Ivory and Obsidian, set the action pace, and Start watching. Pause to inspect the position; Resume continues play. Undo rewinds one computer action and pauses. Reloading restores the saved match paused. You can arrange either side before starting; the computers control all play afterward.

Optional football commentary follows build-up play, attacks, shots and goals, with livelier calls when a chance develops. It is available only at Relaxed · 3 seconds action pace. Switching to Standard or Quick turns it off immediately; returning to Relaxed leaves it off until you choose On. During live play, expect a brief match update about every 10–15 seconds, with important moments taking priority. Shots, pauses and replays can delay the next summary. Live analysis · Hugo + Tom uses Hugo, a local male voice, for fresh analysis of the actual match, while Tom’s expressive saved calls react quickly to shots and goals. Short, energetic football calls accompany attacking play. The model downloads only after you turn commentary on or activate it at kickoff; the first load is about 38 MB including the model and speech runtime. A loading indicator shows progress. If Hugo is loading, slow or unavailable, Tom’s saved calls provide coverage; if those cannot play either, captions remain available. Test voice becomes available when Hugo is ready and plays a fresh Hugo line. British match commentator plays saved audio clips with matching captions. Device voice is another alternative, with Auto preferring natural and enhanced English voices supplied by your browser or device. In British match commentator mode, a saved clip that cannot play may fall back to a device voice. Hugo + Tom mode falls back to captions after Tom. Test voice plays one short call without changing the match; the longer match sample is available before kickoff or while paused. Off stops audio immediately. Pauses, manual replays and dialogs stop stale commentary. If audio is unavailable, match captions still work.

Match conventions

Pieces are never captured. There is no check, castling, en passant, or pawn promotion. Knights kick with one L-shaped jump; other kicks follow their movement directions. Turnovers restart the sequence for the new attacking team. A goal resets the formation and gives kickoff to the conceding side. Most goals at full time wins.

In timed matches, each action has a 30-second deadline for both teams, including the computer. Selecting pieces, rotating the board, or changing settings does not refresh it. Missing the deadline awards the opponent an indirect free kick near the ball, with both teams resettling first. If the defending keeper runs out of time during a shot, it holds position and the shot resolves normally. Pausing or opening a dialog freezes both clocks. Untimed matches have no action deadline and can be ended with Finish match; timed matches finish through the match clock.

At 00:00, the decision already underway finishes before full time. A pending shot or compulsory king release must resolve. A time-wasting award, a foul restart, or a carrying-limit or repetition free kick carries a final attacking chance through the restart and one subsequent attacking round if needed; an indirect kick’s first pass alone does not end that chance. Further missed deadlines during this final chance are played automatically, so play cannot be held open indefinitely. Saved matches and Undo retain the action time and final-chance state.

Model notes

This is a custom game heuristic, tuned for play rather than calibrated to real match data or a published expected-goals fit. Shooting distance, angle, goalkeeper position, and trajectory inform its design; the probability formula and coefficients are our own.

Background: Goalkeeper positioning research ↗ · StatsBomb expected-goals factors ↗

Football rules: IFAB offside ↗ · Throw-ins ↗ · Goal kicks ↗ · Corners ↗. Grid positioning rounds, throw ranges, scatter, and action limits are custom game rules.

The shot-model coefficients, goal-box dimensions, and long-pass accuracy curve are playable defaults for this custom variation and can be revised.
